dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The supplied source addresses federal evidence, appellate and bankruptcy rule amendments, not legal AI capability, verification or work redesign. Although its title references machine-generated evidence, the supplied evidence contains no substantive discussion of that proposal, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: AI evidence: Reliability differs from deepfake authenticity
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central distinction between reliability standards for acknowledged machine-generated evidence under proposed Rule 707 and separate exploratory authentication work for deepfakes under Rule 901. It also confirms that Rule 707 advanced only to publication and public comment, not final adoption, while offering no empirical findings on AI reliability or litigation costs.

This included discussion of a possible new subdivision for  Rule 901 (Authenticating or Identifying Evidence) that would set a framework for evaluating  contentions that an item of evidence has been fabricated using generative AI (deepfakes).

st.t: Amicus transparency: Influence matters alongside legal argument
st.an: The source directly supports targeted amicus transparency: it treats identity, perspective and independence as relevant, endorses disclosure of party influence and covered funding, and narrows the reforms to avoid unjustified burdens and associational-rights concerns rather than pursuing unrestricted disclosure.
qs: For that reason, 191   the Committee thinks that some disclosures about an amicus 192   are important to promote the integrity of court processes and 193   rules.

st.t: Bankruptcy disclosure: Sanctions remain discretionary enforcement
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition. It describes Rule 3001’s disclosure duties, reorganises the rule so sanctions follow those duties, restores sanctions coverage inadvertently narrowed by the 2024 restyling, and confirms that remedies remain discretionary and procedurally safeguarded. It also concerns bankruptcy rules rather than machine-generated evidence.

kp.k: AI evidence prompted three years of rules review
kp.d: The report states that the Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules spent three years considering whether existing Evidence Rules sufficiently regulate the reliability and authenticity of AI-created evidence. This is an account of institutional review, not an empirical finding about AI reliability or a claim that all AI evidence is unreliable.
qs: The Advisory Committee spent three years considering whether the Evidence Rules sufficiently regulate the reliability and authenticity of evidence created by artificial intelligence (AI).

kp.k: Proposed Rule 707 addresses expert-like machine-generated evidence
kp.d: The proposed rule would set admissibility standards for machine-generated evidence that would fall under Rule 702’s expert-testimony requirements if presented through witness testimony. The supplied report describes that scope but does not reproduce Rule 707’s proposed text or specify its detailed requirements; it does not describe a blanket rule for all AI-generated material.
qs: Proposed new Rule 707 sets standards for the admissibility of machine-generated evidence that would be subject to Rule 702’s expert-testimony requirements if testified to by a witness.

kp.k: Rule 707 received publication approval, not final adoption
kp.d: The Advisory Committee recommended publication of proposed Rule 707 for public comment in August 2025. Following minor revisions to the text and committee note, the Standing Committee approved that recommendation with one member objecting. The report therefore records a proposal progressing to public consultation, rather than an enacted evidentiary requirement, and provides no explanation of the objection.
qs: The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules recommended that a proposed amendment to Rule 609 (Impeachment by Evidence of a Criminal Conviction) and a new Rule 707 (Machine-Generated Evidence) be published for public comment in August 2025.

After minor revisions to the text and committee note of each rule, the Standing Committee unanimously approved the Advisory Committee’s recommendation concerning Rule 609 and approved (with one member objecting) the recommendation concerning Rule 707.

kp.k: Deepfake authentication was a separate potential rules initiative
kp.d: At its May 2, 2025 meeting, the Advisory Committee also discussed a possible new subdivision of Rule 901 to establish a framework for evaluating allegations that evidence was fabricated using generative AI. This authentication initiative was distinct from Rule 707’s treatment of expert-like machine-generated evidence and was reported as a discussion item, not an approved amendment.
qs: This included discussion of a possible new subdivision for Rule 901 (Authenticating or Identifying Evidence) that would set a framework for evaluating contentions that an item of evidence has been fabricated using generative AI (deepfakes).

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Standing Committee reports proposed changes to evidence admissibility and possible changes to authentication procedures in response to AI-generated evidence.
pts.d: The report, submitted by Judge John D. Bates as Standing Committee chair, describes proposed Rule 707 as establishing admissibility standards for machine-generated evidence that would fall under Rule 702's expert-testimony requirements if presented through a witness. Separately, it reports the Evidence Advisory Committee's consideration of a possible Rule 901 subdivision addressing allegations of generative-AI fabrication (deepfakes). These are procedural proposals, not findings that AI has already changed litigation outcomes or predictions about legal employment, pricing, or productivity. The supplied document summarizes Rule 707 but does not reproduce its proposed operative text.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis offered is institutional rulemaking deliberation, including three years of consideration; no empirical AI reliability findings are supplied.
pts.d: The report attributes the proposals to the Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules and records the Standing Committee's approval of Rule 707 for publication and public comment, with one member objecting. This documents institutional consideration and procedural action, rather than empirical proof of the extent of AI-related evidentiary problems or the effectiveness of the proposed solution. The AI-related passages contain no datasets, benchmarks, measured error rates, or named cases, and do not explain the objection.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Rule 707 was approved for publication and public comment in August 2025, not final adoption; the deepfake authentication framework remained under discussion.
pts.d: The September 2025 session report records action at the Standing Committee's June 10, 2025 meeting. It specifies August 2025 as the intended publication and comment stage for Rule 707, without stating an effective date or guaranteeing adoption. Its described scope is conditional: machine-generated evidence that would be subject to Rule 702 if testified to by a witness, rather than all AI output. The possible Rule 901 subdivision was discussed at the Evidence Advisory Committee's May 2, 2025 meeting and is presented only as an information item. The report expressly cautions against treating unapproved recommendations as Judicial Conference policy.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposals concern federal courts and parties presenting or contesting machine-generated or allegedly AI-fabricated evidence.
pts.d: The implied affected roles are judges determining admissibility or authentication and litigants and their counsel offering or challenging evidence. Rule 707 would provide standards for admissibility within its stated expert-testimony-related scope; the possible Rule 901 framework would address contentions that evidence is a deepfake. These role-level implications follow from the proposals' stated functions, rather than an express forecast of workload or costs. The report does not specify effects on particular firm types, legal-service providers, client market segments, or access to justice.
